blocks.text: A Mathematics teacher in Enugu has the test scores of forty SS1 students on a scrap of paper. Until those scores sit in a frequency table, a bar chart or a pie chart, they are just a jumble. Presenting data is how you turn a list into something a principal, a parent or an examiner can actually read.

blocks.markdown:
Start with a **tally**. Go through the raw list once, making a mark for each value, and group the marks in fives. The number of marks for each value is its **frequency** $f$. The sum of the frequencies must equal the number of pieces of data: $\sum f = n$.

When the values spread over a wide range, group them into **class intervals** such as $0$–$9$, $10$–$19$, $20$–$29$. The ends of an interval as written are the **class limits**. For drawing a histogram of discrete data, you need the **class boundaries**, which sit halfway between neighbouring classes: the class $10$–$19$ has boundaries $9.5$ and $19.5$.

blocks.title: Class limits and class boundaries
blocks.text: Class limits are the smallest and largest values written in the class (for example 10 and 19). Class boundaries are the true edges used on a histogram axis so that bars touch: 9.5 and 19.5. Mixing the two up leaves gaps in the histogram or plots bars in the wrong place.

blocks.markdown:
### Bar charts, pie charts and histograms

A **bar chart** is for categories or ungrouped values. Bars are separated by gaps; height equals frequency.

A **pie chart** uses a full turn of $360^\circ$. The angle of a sector is

$\text{angle} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360^\circ$.

A **histogram** is for grouped (usually continuous) data. Bars **touch** — there are no gaps — because the axis is a number line of class boundaries. When every class has the same width, bar height equals frequency. When the widths are **unequal**, bar height must be **frequency density**:

$\text{frequency density} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$.

The area of each bar, not its height, then represents the frequency.

blocks.markdown:
### The ogive (cumulative frequency curve)

Add a running total of frequencies to get **cumulative frequency**. Plot each cumulative frequency against the **upper class boundary**, then join the points with a smooth curve. That curve is the **ogive**.

Quartiles are read from the ogive, not guessed from the table:

- $Q_1$ (lower quartile) at cumulative frequency $\frac{n}{4}$
- Median at cumulative frequency $\frac{n}{2}$
- $Q_3$ (upper quartile) at cumulative frequency $\frac{3n}{4}$

From that height on the vertical axis, travel across to the curve and down to the horizontal axis to read the mark.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: On a histogram, bars must touch. If the question gives unequal class widths, you must use frequency density or the areas (and the marks) are wrong. On an ogive, always plot against the upper class boundary — plotting midpoints is a standard way to lose the construction marks.

points: A frequency table is built by tallying raw data; $\sum f$ must equal $n$.
Class limits are the written ends of an interval; class boundaries sit halfway between classes so histogram bars touch.
Bar charts have gaps; pie-chart angles are $\frac{f}{n}\times 360^\circ$; histograms have no gaps.
Unequal class widths need frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
On an ogive, $Q_1$, the median and $Q_3$ are read at $\frac{n}{4}$, $\frac{n}{2}$ and $\frac{3n}{4}$.
